_comment: The world-file build table. One entry per category that ships as a global
FlatGeobuf; `osm/geodata.js` GEO_CATEGORIES stays the source of truth for what a
category MEANS, and this file is the mechanical translation of its Overpass
selector into the two tools the CI build uses.
`filter` is an osmium tags-filter expression list. It is deliberately WIDER than
the selector: osmium tags-filter cannot express negation or presence-of-a-second-
key, so it does the cheap key=value cut and `where` does the rest. Widening is
safe (a superset is filtered down later); narrowing silently loses features, so
never move a condition from `where` into `filter` without checking it is
expressible.
`where` is OGR SQL evaluated against the exported attributes. Field names are the
raw OSM keys, so `natural` needs quoting. It must reproduce the Overpass selector
EXACTLY — this is the line that decides whether a world-file run and an Overpass
run give the same answer, and a mismatch is silent.
`post` names a Python predicate in build.py's POST_FILTERS that runs after `where`,
for the one condition OGR SQL cannot express: parsing a maxspeed string. Absent
for every other category.
`geometry` is the per-layer `osmium export --geometry-types` list, and it is the
double-emit fix (PLAN.md Phase 0): osmium exports a closed way ONCE PER REQUESTED
TYPE, so asking every layer for point,linestring,polygon wrote every closed way
twice — its polygon plus the same ring as a zero-area linestring — inflating
counts up to 2x. The class is derived from the selector and OSM tagging reality:
point           the filter only admits nodes (mountain, bench).
point,polygon   area tags. A closed way exports once, as its polygon; an
UNCLOSED way carrying an area tag is a mapping error and is
dropped (Overpass would have returned it as a stray line).
point,linestring,polygon + dedup
genuinely mixed layers — a lake is a polygon and a river a
linestring in the same file — where the linestring reading must
survive, so build.py drops a way's linestring only when the
same way was also exported as a polygon.
THE point,polygon AUDIT. `point,polygon` is a claim about OSM tagging — that no
mapper legitimately draws this feature as an open way — and getting it wrong loses
features with no error anywhere. Every layer in that class was re-checked against
its selector's tagging semantics AND measured on two extracts with different
mapping cultures (Michigan and Germany), counting distinct entities that export as
a linestring and never as a polygon — i.e. exactly what the class drops:
advertising      56/772 (7.3%) MI, 816/35,816 (2.3%) DE  → RECLASSIFIED, mixed.
The only structural loss. See its own comment.
shelter          0 MI, 24/99,512 (0.02%) DE              → kept point,polygon
pitch            0 MI, 61/453,498 (0.01%) DE             → kept point,polygon
park             0 MI, 2/14,196 DE                       → kept point,polygon
shop             1/27,295 MI, 0/486,941 DE               → kept point,polygon
place_of_worship 0 MI, 1/72,054 DE                       → kept point,polygon
fast_food        0 MI, 1/44,034 DE                       → kept point,polygon
park museum movie_theater hospital library zoo aquarium amusement_park
golf_course foreign_consulate commercial_airport rail_station toilets grocery
newsagent restaurant cafe                                → exactly 0 on both
The kept ones are all the same judgement, and it is deliberate rather than a
tolerance threshold: `amenity`, `tourism`, `shop`, `office`, `leisure`, `landuse`,
`aeroway=aerodrome` and `railway=station` describe a place, and OSM documents no
linear form for any of them — an open way carrying one is a mapping error, which
is what the residual handful are (Michigan's single `shop` open way was inspected
and is one). Overpass would have returned them as stray unrenderable lines; a POI
placed on such a line is worse than its absence. Whereas the keys that DO have a
documented linear form are, all of them, already mixed: advertising, railway=
platform / public_transport=platform, natural=coastline, waterway=river/canal,
railway=rail.
`admin` is deliberately NOT in this table at all — see `_admin_comment` below.
One more thing this class drops, and the measurement above already counts it: a
CLOSED way tagged `area=no` is a linestring to osmium regardless of its other tags,
so it never reaches a point,polygon layer either. It is folded into the numbers
above and is a rounding error in both extracts.
`green` is in the mixed class for an exactness reason, not a tagging one: it is a
term of the curse_animal_habitat partition identity (see _curse_comment), which
holds feature-for-feature only if every term counts each OSM object exactly once.
Dropping green's unclosed-way mapping errors while the count-only terms keep
theirs would break the identity by exactly those errors.
`count_only: true` marks a layer the client only ever COUNTS via the R-tree
(worldCount reads no feature bytes). build.py ships those as 2-point bbox-diagonal
linestrings with no properties — identical envelopes, so every search result is
unchanged (PLAN.md Phase 1 R1) — and dedups them on (osm_type, osm_id).
The genuinely dense categories — building, street, footpath, car_street, bridge,
tree — are NOT here. They are counts, not icons, and shipping their geometry
globally is tens of gigabytes in service of tallies. They build into the sparse
density grid instead; see `density` below.
restaurant, cafe, fast_food and shop were also once on that exclusion list and are
back as real features on purpose. They are not dense at planet scale (~2M
restaurants worldwide), and `cuisineDetail` in osm/geodata.js reads the `cuisine`
tag off individual restaurant features — a grid cell cannot answer that.

categories.where: leisure = 'park' AND name IS NOT NULL
tourism = 'museum' AND name IS NOT NULL
amenity = 'cinema' AND name IS NOT NULL
amenity = 'hospital' AND name IS NOT NULL
amenity = 'library' AND name IS NOT NULL
leisure = 'golf_course' AND name IS NOT NULL AND (golf IS NULL OR golf <> 'driving_range')
office = 'diplomatic' AND diplomatic IN ('consulate', 'consulate_general') AND (consulate IS NULL OR consulate <> 'honorary')
aeroway = 'aerodrome' AND iata IS NOT NULL
"natural" IN ('peak', 'volcano') AND name IS NOT NULL

_comment: The selector is `railway=rail AND highspeed=yes`, with a documented fallback to
`maxspeed >= 200 km/h` accepting '200', '200 km/h' and '125 mph'. OGR SQL cannot
parse those strings, so `where` keeps every candidate carrying EITHER key and the
`highspeed` post-filter does the numeric comparison in Python. Dropping the post
step would tag every ordinary rail line on Earth as high-speed.
Mixed geometry: rail ways are linear, but a closed way (a test loop, a balloon
loop) exports as a polygon too, and the linestring reading must survive for every
open way — so this takes the dedup route rather than a polygon-only export.
categories.where: railway = 'rail' AND (highspeed = 'yes' OR maxspeed IS NOT NULL)

_comment: Genuinely mixed: named lakes are polygons, rivers and canals are linestrings,
and a handful of natural=water nodes exist. The dedup drops the zero-area
linestring copy of every closed lake way.
categories.where: ("natural" = 'water' AND name IS NOT NULL AND (water IS NULL OR water NOT IN ('pool', 'reflecting_pool')) AND (leisure IS NULL OR leisure <> 'swimming_pool')) OR (waterway IN ('river', 'canal') AND name IS NOT NULL)

_comment: Coastline ways are linear shore segments, but a small island IS one closed
natural=coastline way, which exports as both a polygon and its ring — hence
mixed with dedup rather than linestring-only, which would change what a closed
island way ships as.
Genuinely mixed: platforms are mapped as nodes, as linear ways along the
platform edge, and as areas. The linear form is common and must survive.
Genuinely mixed, and the one layer the point,polygon class got WRONG. An
`advertising=*` value describes a physical object, not a piece of land, so
`area=*` semantics never apply to it and mappers draw a billboard's FACE as a
short two-node way — a valid, documented mapping, not an error. Classified
point,polygon those ways were never exported at all: 56 of 772 distinct
entities lost in Michigan (7.3%) and 816 of 35,816 in Germany (2.3%), silently.
Sampled losses are `advertising=billboard` / `sign` / `yes` on open ways.
So it takes the platform route — all three types plus the dedup pass — which
keeps the linear faces AND still collapses the closed billboard structures that
osmium double-emits.
Mixed for the R2 identity, not for tagging reality: landuse is an area tag, but
green is the positive term of the curse_animal_habitat partition (see
_curse_comment) and the identity is exact only if every term counts each OSM
object exactly once — including the unclosed-way mapping errors the count-only
terms keep as single records.
restaurant carries the `cuisine` tag that Curse of the Distant Cuisine counts off
individual features. It must stay a feature category — a density cell cannot say
which country's cuisine is served inside it.

_curse_comment: CURSE_PREDICATE_SELECTORS in osm/geodata.js are map-wide COUNTS, not features, and
several of them deliberately differ from the same-named GEO_CATEGORIES selector —
curse `water` says 'marked', the category says 'named', and the two differ by 8:1.
Where a curse predicate is exactly a shipped category the client re-counts that
file; the ones below are the ones that are NOT, so they get their own layer. They
are counted, never drawn, so they carry `count_only` and ship as bbox diagonals
with no properties (PLAN.md Phase 1 R1).
curse `bridge`, `car_street` and `building` are answered by the density grid, and
curse `grocery`, `shop`, `print_source` and `tumble_ground` are exactly the
grocery / shop / newsagent / pitch category files.
curse_animal_habitat is DELETED (PLAN.md Phase 1 R2) — it was 45% a copy of
`green`. Its count is reconstructed client-side as an exact partition identity:
count(curse_animal_habitat)
== count(green) - count(green_recreation_ground) + count(animal_delta)
with the old selector
A = leisure IN (park, nature_reserve)
OR landuse IN (forest, grass, meadow, village_green)
OR (natural = water AND name)
and green G = landuse IN (forest, grass, meadow, village_green,
recreation_ground). `landuse` is single-valued, so G minus its recreation_ground
members is EXACTLY A's landuse line, and animal_delta is exactly A's other two
lines with the landuse-line members removed — no feature is counted twice and
none is missed. Both derived layers are count_only diagonals over UNCHANGED
envelopes, so the identity holds for every bbox the R-tree is asked about.
See CURSE_ANIMAL_HABITAT_TERMS in osm/geodata.js, which consumes this identity.

curse_layers.where: ("natural" = 'water' AND (water IS NULL OR water NOT IN ('pool', 'reflecting_pool')) AND (leisure IS NULL OR leisure <> 'swimming_pool')) OR landuse IN ('reservoir', 'basin') OR waterway IN ('river', 'canal')
leisure IN ('park', 'garden', 'playground') OR amenity IN ('library', 'place_of_worship', 'marketplace', 'townhall') OR highway = 'pedestrian'

_comment: R2 subtraction term: green's recreation_ground members, ALL of them —
single-valued landuse makes count(green) minus this exactly the habitat
selector's landuse line.
R2 addition term: the habitat selector's leisure and named-water lines, with
features already counted by green's landuse line excluded so the identity
never double-counts. recreation_ground members are NOT excluded here — they
are cancelled by the subtraction term instead.
curse_layers.where: (leisure IN ('park', 'nature_reserve') OR ("natural" = 'water' AND name IS NOT NULL)) AND (landuse IS NULL OR landuse NOT IN ('forest', 'grass', 'meadow', 'village_green'))

_density_comment: The categories that are tallies rather than icons. Their planet-wide geometry is
tens of gigabytes and every question asked of them is a count, so they build into
one sparse grid instead: a FlatGeobuf of POINTS, one per populated cell, carrying
an integer column per category. Same file format, same R-tree, same HTTP Range
client as everything else — a bbox query over it returns the cells the map covers
and the counts are summed client-side. A zero-valued count is OMITTED from its
cell (PLAN.md Phase 1 R4): `worldDensity` skips zeros on read, so absent == 0 by
construction and the bytes are pure savings.
THIS IS AN APPROXIMATION AND IT REPLACES AN EXACT NUMBER. Today `building` is
fetched as points and counted per zone exactly. A cell is attributed to a zone when
its CENTRE falls inside the zone circle, so a cell straddling the circle edge lands
wholly in or wholly out. At `cell_deg` = 0.002 (~220 m at the equator) against the
~400 m zone radius that is a boundary error on the order of a tenth of the circle's
area. Map-wide counts — which is what every curse predicate and the street-density
figure actually read — stay exact: they are a sum over every cell in the bbox and
no feature is counted twice, because each is attributed to exactly one cell.
`osm/geodata.js` marks per-zone density figures approximate in provenance. Do not
quietly present them as measured counts.
street and car_street overlap by design (a residential road is both); they are
separate columns because Right Turn, Luxury Car and the street-density figure ask
different questions, and CAR_STREET_SELECTOR is the constant that keeps them honest.

layers.where: highway IS NOT NULL AND highway NOT IN ('motorway', 'motorway_link', 'trunk_link', 'construction', 'proposed', 'raceway')

highway IN ('motorway', 'trunk', 'primary', 'secondary', 'tertiary', 'unclassified', 'residential', 'living_street', 'service', 'motorway_link', 'trunk_link', 'primary_link', 'secondary_link', 'tertiary_link') AND (motor_vehicle IS NULL OR motor_vehicle <> 'no') AND (access IS NULL OR access <> 'no')
bridge IS NOT NULL AND bridge <> 'no' AND (highway IS NOT NULL OR railway IS NOT NULL)

_admin_comment: There is NO `admin` entry in this table, and its absence is the point. The
shipped world still HAS an admin layer — the polygon layer of administrative
areas that `adminInfo` in osm/geodata.js reads for containment, country codes
and ISO3166-2 — but it comes from Overture's already-assembled division_area
(build-admin.sh), placed into the merged world by merge.py --admin, which stamps
`admin_source: "overture"`. See README §'The admin layer comes from Overture,
not OSM'.
An OSM admin entry used to live here, and building it per shard is broken by
construction: an administrative relation only assembles into a polygon when it
fits entirely inside the extract, so a Michigan extract yields 73 level-2
features — all zero-area fragments and no USA polygon. merge.py accordingly
never merges admin from shards; every per-shard admin.fgb was built, indexed
and uploaded only to be discarded, measured at 16.5% of pooled feature-shard
output (125 MB on one European shard). Removing the entry — rather than adding
a skip flag every caller must remember — is what makes the waste impossible to
reintroduce by forgetting a flag.
Consequences of the removal, so nobody re-derives them: build.py's full table
is now 36 layers and no build.py output ever contains admin; merge.py's full
manifest is still 37 (it hardcodes admin into its layer universe and fills it
from --admin); admin_level / boundary / ISO3166-* stay in include_tags and
runtime_columns untouched, because changing those lists changes the bytes of
every other layer for no benefit.
_include_tags_comment: The tag columns osmium export writes. Pinning this list is what gives the
GeoJSONSeq a stable schema, which is what lets ogr2ogr build a FlatGeobuf without
scanning the whole stream to discover fields. Every key referenced by any `where`
above MUST appear here, plus everything in runtime_columns.
_runtime_columns_comment: What actually SHIPS on a feature (PLAN.md Phase 1 R5): the columns the client
reads at runtime, verified by grepping osm/*.js and rules/score.js —
osm_type/osm_id   identity: featuresToPois, every tie-break sort, and the
Phase-3 shard merge's dedup key. Never strip at shard level.
name:en           the admin ladder prefers it (geodata.js adminInfo)
cuisine           Curse of the Distant Cuisine (cuisineTokens)
Everything else in include_tags exists only so a `where` clause can see it, and
ogr2ogr -select projects it away per layer (intersected with the columns the
layer's features actually carry, because -select hard-fails on a missing field).
